scope: Two different briefs against the same synthetic lease. Planning proposals are used as agreed inputs for this engineering evaluation; no lawyer/user approval is implied. Chat continuity has model-free tests. Mechanical checks do not establish legal accuracy.

cases.objective: Help my tenant understand whether exiting in 2029 is feasible. Prepare a short client update covering break conditions, costs, missing facts and next enquiries; do not confirm compliance.

brief.outcome: A client update addressing the tenant's feasibility question on a 2029 exit by mapping key break and termination conditions in the lease, identifying exit-related costs and liabilities, flagging material gaps in lease documentation, and setting out immediate enquiries needed to assess compliance and realistic exit options.
priorities: Identify all break clauses, break conditions and break dates in the lease—particularly any opportunities within or before 2029
Map exit-related costs and liabilities (dilapidations, reinstatement, rent, service charge, rates, insurance) to understand total exit cost
Confirm lease term structure and review dates to verify whether 2029 aligns with a contractual break or natural lease end
Assess compliance obligations (repairing covenants, use restrictions, alienation clauses) that could create barriers to or costs for exit
open_questions: Does the lease contain a break clause exercisable by the tenant (or jointly with landlord) at 2029 or any earlier date, and if so, what notice period and conditions apply?
What remedial works, reinstatement or dilapidations obligations bind the tenant at termination, and have any schedules of condition or dilapidations schedule been agreed?
Are there any restrictions on assignment, subletting or change of use that would prevent a commercial exit strategy (e.g., sale of lease or disposal of business)?
What other material lease terms (rent review mechanisms, insurance obligations, service charge caps, guarantor requirements) affect the cost and feasibility of exit?

sections.title: Current Lease Structure & Term
sections.purpose: Confirm the lease commencement date (1 January 2024), full term length (15 years to 2039), review dates (2029 and 2034), and whether 2029 marks any contractual break point or only a rent review

sections.title: Break Clauses & Exit Triggers
sections.purpose: Identify and summarize any break clauses available to the tenant (or jointly) at 2029 or earlier, including notice periods, conditions precedent, and whether exercise must coincide with a review date

sections.title: Exit Costs & Liabilities
sections.purpose: Outline categories of cost and liability on exit: rent through termination, service charge, rates, insurance, dilapidations, reinstatement works, and any other landlord claims; flag unknowns

brief.objective: Help my tenant understand whether exiting in 2029 is feasible. Prepare a short client update covering break conditions, costs, missing facts and next enquiries; do not confirm compliance.

findings.title: Break Clause Available at 1 January 2029 with Twelve-Month Notice and Three Conditions
findings.interpretation: The Tenant has a contractual right to determine the Lease on 1 January 2029 (the fifth anniversary of commencement), making a 2029 exit theoretically feasible from a contractual standpoint. However, the break is conditional and requires strict compliance with three preconditions: no material unremedied breach of the Tenant's covenants, vacant possession of the entire premises, and payment of a 'Break Premium' equal to six months' rent (at the rate payable immediately before the break date). The notice requirement is 12 months' prior written notice, which must be served in accordance with Section 196 of the Law of Property Act 1925; once given, a Break Notice is irrevocable. The second break date is 1 January 2034 (the tenth anniversary), but 2029 is the material near-term opportunity.
findings.relevance: This is the primary lever for a 2029 exit. To understand feasibility, the Tenant must assess: (a) whether it will be in material breach of its covenants by the break date; (b) whether it can secure vacant possession of all three floors; and (c) whether it can afford the Break Premium (currently not ascertainable without knowing the reviewed rent as at 1 January 2029). A breach of the break conditions will render the Break Notice of no effect, forcing the Lease to continue until 31 December 2038 (the contractual expiry date). Assignment or subletting of the lease does not eliminate this liability—the original tenant remains bound unless formally released.
findings.next_step: Conduct a detailed dilapidations and compliance review to identify any material breaches of the Tenant's covenants (repair, decoration, use restrictions, insurance obligations) that may not be remediable by 1 January 2029. Confirm the business and occupancy plan: can the Tenant achieve vacant possession by the break date? Request the Landlord's current position on any alleged breaches. Once the reviewed rent is set at 1 January 2029, calculate the Break Premium (six months at that reviewed rate) to determine the cash cost of exercise.
findings.quote: The Tenant may determine this Lease on the fifth (5th) anniversary of the Term Commencement Date (being 1 January 2029) or the tenth (10th) anniversary of the Term Commencement Date (being 1 January 2034) (each a "Break Date") by serving written notice on the Landlord in accordance with clause 8.2... The Tenant must give the Landlord not less than twelve (12) months' prior written notice of its intention to exercise a break right (a "Break Notice"). A Break Notice, once given, shall be irrevocable... The Tenant's right to determine this Lease on a Break Date shall be conditional upon the following conditions being satisfied on or before the relevant Break Date: (a) there is no material breach by the Tenant of any of the Tenant's covenants in this Lease which remains unremedied at the Break Date; (b) the Tenant gives vacant possession of the whole of the Premises to the Landlord on or before the Break Date, free from all occupiers, subtenants and other persons claiming through or under the Tenant; (c) the Tenant pays to the Landlord on or before the Break Date a sum equivalent to six (6) months' rent at the rate payable immediately before the Break Date (the "Break Premium"), such payment to be made by way of cleared funds.
findings.uncertainty: The exact amount of the Break Premium cannot be confirmed until the Reviewed Rent is ascertained at 1 January 2029 (an upward-only review). The Tenant's current Initial Rent is £850,000 per annum (exclusive of VAT), meaning the Break Premium on that basis would be £425,000, but this will likely increase. The definition of 'material breach' is not defined in the lease; this is a judgment call and could become disputed if the Tenant believes a breach is minor or has been substantially remedied. The notice-service mechanics under Section 196 LPA 1925 require verification of proper serving procedures. The Lease does not state a time for payment of the Break Premium (on or before the Break Date), and 'cleared funds' suggests same-day payment.

findings.title: Repairing and Decoration Obligations with Schedule of Condition—Key Compliance Risk
findings.interpretation: The Tenant has ongoing full repairing obligations throughout the Term with 'fair wear and tear' excepted. This includes keeping the interior (internal surfaces of external and load-bearing walls, floors, ceilings, columns, doors, windows and frames) properly decorated to a 'first-class office building in the City of London' standard. Crucially, the Tenant must redecorate at least once every five years AND in the last year of the Term (however it is determined—i.e., whether by expiry on 31 December 2038 or by break exercise on 1 January 2029). The Tenant is bound to 'yield up' the Premises in good and substantial repair and condition at expiration or sooner determination. A Schedule of Condition was prepared by Carter Mitchell Surveyors LLP at the Term Commencement Date (1 January 2024) and is annexed as Schedule 4; the Tenant's repairing obligations do not require the Premises to be put in any better condition than shown in that schedule.
findings.relevance: These obligations create a critical compliance and cost barrier to a 2029 break. If the Tenant exercises the break on 1 January 2029 without being in full repair and proper decorative condition, or without having fully redecorated (since the last decoration cycle), it will likely be in material breach and the Break Notice will be ineffective. The 'last year' redecoration requirement is particularly onerous: a 2029 break means 2028 is the last year, so a full professional redecoration (internal surfaces only, but including all walls, floors, ceilings, doors and frames to first-class standard) must be completed by 31 December 2028. Failure exposes the Tenant to a failed break and a further nine years of the Lease to 31 December 2038. Additionally, any defects beyond fair wear and tear will need remediation, or the Landlord may pursue a dilapidations claim after termination.
findings.next_step: Instruct a qualified surveyor (if not already done) to inspect the Premises against the Schedule of Condition (Schedule 4) to establish a current dilapidations profile. Identify any item that is in worse condition than recorded in the schedule, or is beyond fair wear and tear, and estimate the cost and timeline to remedy each by 1 January 2029. Plan and cost a full professional redecoration of all internal surfaces to first-class office standard, scheduled for 2028 to meet the 'last year' requirement. Obtain quotations for these works. Flag to the Tenant that these remedial works are a prerequisite to break exercise and are unrecoverable costs if the break cannot be exercised.
findings.quote: The Tenant shall keep the Premises and every part thereof (including all additions and alterations thereto) in good and substantial repair and condition throughout the Term, fair wear and tear excepted, and shall yield up the Premises in such repair and condition at the expiration or sooner determination of the Term. The Tenant shall keep the interior of the Premises (including the internal surfaces of all external and load-bearing walls, floors, ceilings, columns, doors, windows and window frames) properly decorated to a standard consistent with that of a first-class office building in the City of London, and shall redecorate the same not less frequently than once in every five (5) years of the Term and in the last year of the Term (howsoever determined).
findings.uncertainty: The standard of 'first-class office building in the City of London' is qualitative and may be disputed; market conditions and Landlord expectations at 1 January 2029 will influence enforcement risk. 'Fair wear and tear' is a flexible standard and disputes over whether specific defects fall within it are common. The Schedule of Condition is referenced but not reproduced in the extracts reviewed; its level of detail and any ambiguities will directly impact the scope of remedial work required. The timing and phasing of redecoration across three large floors (32,500 sq ft total) within the 'last year' will require careful planning to minimise business disruption and avoid any claim that the Tenant has not completed the work by the break date.

findings.title: Break Premium Cost and Upward-Only Rent Review at 1 January 2029
findings.interpretation: The Break Premium is stipulated as six months' rent at the rate payable immediately before the Break Date (1 January 2029). This means six months of the Reviewed Rent applicable from 1 January 2029, not the Initial Rent (£850,000 per annum). The Lease contains an upward-only rent review mechanism: the Reviewed Rent at 1 January 2029 is the higher of (a) the rent payable before the review date (£850,000 per annum) and (b) the open market rent of the Premises as at 1 January 2029. The open market rent is assessed by reference to willing landlord/willing tenant principles, assuming the Premises are fit for immediate occupation, unoccupied by the Tenant, all covenants are fully observed, and no improvements carried out by the Tenant have added value. If the parties cannot agree on the Reviewed Rent by 1 January 2029, an independent surveyor will determine it, acting as an expert (not arbitrator). Pending ascertainment, the Tenant continues to pay the previous rate (£850,000) plus interest at 2% above Barclays base rate on any shortfall, once determined.
findings.relevance: The Break Premium is a direct cash cost that the Tenant must pay to exercise the break. At the current Initial Rent of £850,000 per annum, a notional Break Premium would be £425,000. However, if the open market rent at 1 January 2029 is higher (as is reasonably foreseeable given inflation and upward-only review), the Break Premium will be higher. For example, if the Reviewed Rent is £900,000, the Break Premium becomes £450,000. This is a material financial commitment and will affect the Tenant's decision-making on exit feasibility. The Tenant must budget for this cost. Additionally, the interest payable on any shortfall between the rent currently paid (£850,000) and the Reviewed Rent (from the review date until payment) is an additional, harder-to-quantify cost.
findings.next_step: Engage a commercial property surveyor to provide a valuation forecast for the Premises at 1 January 2029, applying open market rent principles (as defined in clause 3.2.2 to 3.2.4). This will provide an estimate of the likely Reviewed Rent and hence the Break Premium. Factor this cost into the Tenant's exit budget. Consider whether the Tenant should initiate early discussions with the Landlord on the Reviewed Rent (to avoid surveyor determination costs and delay) or pre-emptively gather evidence for a surveyor determination if the parties are likely to differ materially. Clarify the Landlord's current view of market rent to inform strategy.
findings.quote: The Tenant shall pay to the Landlord the Initial Rent of Eight Hundred and Fifty Thousand Pounds (£850,000) per annum, without any deduction, counterclaim or set-off whatsoever... With effect from each Review Date, the rent payable shall be the higher of (a) the rent payable immediately before the relevant Review Date and (b) the open market rent of the Premises as at the relevant Review Date, determined in accordance with clauses 3.2.2 to 3.2.5 below (the "Reviewed Rent")... the Tenant pays to the Landlord on or before the Break Date a sum equivalent to six (6) months' rent at the rate payable immediately before the Break Date (the "Break Premium"), such payment to be made by way of cleared funds.
findings.uncertainty: The actual Reviewed Rent at 1 January 2029 is uncertain; it depends on office market conditions, the occupancy and condition of the Premises at that date, and comparable evidence. The lease text does not specify the date by which the Reviewed Rent must be formally determined; if there is dispute, a surveyor will need to be appointed, which may delay confirmation of the Break Premium amount. The interest calculation on any rent shortfall and its timing is also not explicitly detailed, creating a minor cash-flow uncertainty.

findings.title: Service Charge and Insurance Costs; Tenant's Proportion 18.7%
findings.interpretation: The Tenant is liable for a share of the Landlord's obligations to maintain the structure, exterior, plant, machinery and equipment serving the Building (including lifts, air conditioning, fire systems, and common lighting). The Tenant's proportion is 18.7%, representing the ratio of the net internal area of the Premises (approximately 32,500 square feet) to the total lettable area of the Building. This service charge is recoverable from the Tenant and constitutes additional rent. Additionally, the Tenant must reimburse the Landlord on demand a fair proportion (18.7%) of the insurance premium paid for the full reinstatement value of the Building, including professional fees, demolition and site clearance costs, and VAT, plus any applicable excess under the policy. These reimbursements also constitute additional rent. The Tenant must not do anything that may render void or voidable any insurance policy or cause increased premiums.
findings.relevance: Service charge and insurance are ongoing annual costs, in addition to rent, and will be payable up to and including the break date (1 January 2029). The Tenant is liable for these charges as additional rent, meaning failure to pay could trigger a breach and jeopardise the break. The 18.7% share suggests this is a multi-let building; the Tenant's charges are proportionate. At break, the Tenant should ensure all service charge and insurance arrears (if any) are settled to avoid a default. The costs also factor into the total ongoing cost of the lease up to the break date and should be included in the exit budget.
findings.next_step: Obtain the current annual service charge budget and insurance premium from the Landlord or the managing agent, and verify the Tenant's 18.7% share. Request historical service charge statements and insurance invoices for the past 2–3 years to forecast likely charges through to 1 January 2029. Establish whether the lease contains any cap on service charge increases or if it is uncapped. Ensure that the Tenant's accounting systems flag all service charge and insurance invoices for payment and set aside funds to ensure no arrears accrue at break. Clarify the process and timing for service charge and insurance settlements at or around the break date.
findings.quote: The cost of the Landlord's obligations under this clause 4.2 shall be recoverable from the Tenant as part of the service charge in accordance with Schedule 3 hereto, the Tenant's proportion being 18.7% (representing the ratio of the net internal area of the Premises to the total lettable area of the Building). [Section 5] The Tenant shall reimburse to the Landlord on demand a fair proportion (being the Tenant's proportion as defined in clause 4.2.3) of the premium paid or payable by the Landlord for such insurance and any excess applicable under the policy. Such reimbursement shall constitute additional rent payable under this Lease.
findings.uncertainty: The service charge budget and actual annual charges are not set out in the lease extracts reviewed; Schedule 3 governs the service charge detail and is not provided. Likewise, the current insurance premium is not stated. Historical and forecast service charge and insurance costs are needed to quantify the ongoing burden to the break date. The lease does not specify whether there is any adjustment or apportionment of service charge and insurance on termination (e.g., whether the Tenant must contribute to charges only up to the break date or until the end of the calendar quarter/year).

findings.title: Assignment and Subletting Restrictions; No Partial Subletting Permitted
findings.interpretation: The Tenant may not assign the whole of the Lease without the prior written consent of the Landlord, such consent not to be unreasonably withheld or delayed. The Landlord may impose reasonable conditions, including a requirement for an Authorised Guarantee Agreement (AGA) from the outgoing Tenant. The Landlord is not obliged to consent unless the proposed assignee has demonstrated sufficient financial standing and is a respectable and responsible entity. The Tenant may sublet the whole of the Premises (not any part), again subject to the Landlord's prior written consent (not to be unreasonably withheld), provided that any subletting is at a rent not less than the higher of the current rent under the lease and the then open market rent. Sub-leases must contain provisions for upward-only rent review at intervals of not more than five years and must be consistent with the terms of the head lease. Critically, the Tenant is prohibited from subletting any part of the Premises; the whole must be sublet as a single unit.
findings.relevance: These restrictions materially constrain the Tenant's commercial exit options. The Tenant cannot execute an exit strategy that involves a partial disposal or split occupancy (e.g., subletting one floor while vacating the others). If the Tenant cannot achieve outright vacation by 1 January 2029, subletting is the only alternative to holding the lease to term, but any subletting must be of the entire three-floor space as a whole, at a minimum rent, and is subject to Landlord consent. Additionally, if the Tenant assigns the lease, the Landlord may require an AGA, which means the outgoing Tenant remains liable if the assignee defaults. Lastly, subletting does not extinguish the Tenant's primary obligations under the Lease (rent, service charge, repair, insurance); the Tenant remains liable even after subletting, unless it exercises the break and terminates its lease entirely.
findings.next_step: Clarify the Tenant's commercial exit strategy: (a) is the goal to vacate the entire premises by 1 January 2029 (in which case assignment or subletting of the whole lease is an exit route only if the break cannot be exercised)? (b) or does the Tenant's business plan require occupying part of the space and disposing of the remainder? If the latter, the Lease does not permit this, and the Tenant would need to negotiate a deed of variation with the Landlord to permit partial subletting, or accept continued liability for the whole demised space. Establish whether there is any prospective market demand for subletting the entire space at a rent meeting the minimum threshold. Verify whether the Tenant has received any prior Landlord consents or AGAs that may affect assignment strategy.
findings.quote: The Tenant shall not assign the whole or any part of this Lease without the prior written consent of the Landlord, such consent not to be unreasonably withheld or delayed. The Landlord may impose reasonable conditions on any such consent, including (without limitation) a requirement for an authorised guarantee agreement from the outgoing Tenant... The Tenant shall not sublet the whole of the Premises without the prior written consent of the Landlord, such consent not to be unreasonably withheld or delayed, provided that any subletting shall be at a rent not less than the higher of the rent payable under this Lease and the then open market rent of the Premises... The Tenant shall not sublet any part of the Premises (as distinct from the whole).
findings.uncertainty: The process, timing and criteria for obtaining Landlord consent to assignment or subletting are not detailed in the lease extracts reviewed; this may depend on Landlord practice or prior correspondence. The definition of 'reasonable conditions' and 'respectable and responsible entity' are subjective; disputes over Landlord consent could arise. The enforceability of an AGA and the Tenant's residual liability post-assignment are not addressed in the lease extracts and would require analysis of the Law of Property (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1994. The current market demand for subletting the entire space (32,500 sq ft) at a competitive rent is unknown.

findings.title: Lease Term Expiry and No Automatic Renewal; Manual Surrender or Landlord Claims Required at Termination
findings.interpretation: The Lease is for a fixed term of 15 years commencing on 1 January 2024 and expiring on 31 December 2038, subject to earlier determination in accordance with the lease provisions (i.e., by exercise of the break on 1 January 2029 or 1 January 2034). The lease contains no provision for automatic renewal or extension. On expiry (whether by the natural end date of 31 December 2038 or by exercise of a break clause at 1 January 2029 or 1 January 2034), the Tenant is required to yield up the Premises to the Landlord in good and substantial repair and condition, free from all occupiers, subtenants and other persons. If the Tenant fails to yield up the Premises in the required condition, the Landlord is entitled to pursue dilapidations claims and other remedies (including forfeiture for breach, if applicable). The Lease does not contain an express provision for a formal surrender deed or delivery of keys; these are likely matters of custom and convention, but the lease text requires 'yield up' of the Premises.
findings.relevance: This is critical context for a 2029 exit. If the Tenant exercises the break successfully, the Lease will terminate on 1 January 2029, and no further rent or service charge will be payable after that date. However, if the Tenant fails to achieve a successful break (due to breach, failure to give notice, or inability to pay the Break Premium), the Lease will continue to 31 December 2038. The long tail of liability (nine additional years) creates a significant financial and operational risk if the 2029 break is not executed properly. At termination (break or expiry), the Tenant's repairing and decorating obligations do not end; they intensify. The Tenant must yield up in the required condition, and the Landlord may pursue dilapidations claims after termination if the Premises are not returned in the stated condition.
findings.next_step: Confirm with the Landlord the procedure and requirements for yielding up the Premises at the break date (formal notice, surrender deed, keys, final inspection). Verify whether the Landlord intends to pursue a professional dilapidations schedule or survey at termination (standard practice in commercial leases). Establish the Tenant's plan for evacuation, removal of tenant's fixtures, and making good of any alterations or damage. Understand that any dilapidations claim can be pursued by the Landlord after the Lease has terminated, with interest and professional fees, and plan accordingly. Ensure the Tenant's business plan includes a realistic relocation timeline and all associated costs (moving, lease-up at alternative premises, interim occupancy, etc.).
findings.quote: The Term shall be for a period of fifteen (15) years commencing on 1 January 2024 and expiring on 31 December 2038, subject to earlier determination in accordance with the provisions of this Lease. [Section 4.1.1] The Tenant shall keep the Premises and every part thereof (including all additions and alterations thereto) in good and substantial repair and condition throughout the Term, fair wear and tear excepted, and shall yield up the Premises in such repair and condition at the expiration or sooner determination of the Term.
findings.uncertainty: The Lease does not provide an express procedure or timeline for formal yield-up or for the Landlord to issue a final dilapidations claim. Commercial practice typically allows the Landlord a period (often 12 weeks to 6 months post-termination) to quantify dilapidations; the lease is silent on this. Post-break liability for dilapidations is also not explicitly qualified in the extracts reviewed, although it is implied. The interaction between the Tenant's repairing obligations throughout the Term and its yield-up obligations at termination (e.g., whether certain works must be completed during the Term or can be deferred) is not clarified.

gaps: No schedule of condition (Schedule 4) or dilapidations profile has been reviewed; this is critical to assessing the cost and feasibility of achieving break-ready condition by 1 January 2029
The current Initial Rent of £850,000 per annum is stated, but the anticipated Reviewed Rent at 1 January 2029 is unknown; a commercial property valuation is essential to forecast the Break Premium
The service charge budget, historical charges, and any caps or escalation mechanisms are not provided; Schedule 3 (service charge schedule) has not been reviewed
The current insurance premium and any anticipated changes to the Tenant's reimbursement obligation are not stated

The Lease contains references to Schedule 1 (rights granted), Schedule 2 (reserved rights), and Schedule 3 (service charge mechanism), none of which have been reviewed in detail; these may contain material conditions affecting exit
No information on whether any guarantor or parental company has given security for the Lease, or what happens to guarantor liability if the break is successfully exercised
The Landlord's current position on any alleged breaches of the Tenant's covenants is unknown; this is essential to assess compliance risk for break exercise
No information on the Tenant's occupancy plans, relocation timeline, or business continuity requirements, which will drive the feasibility and cost of exit planning

cases.draft:
**CLIENT UPDATE: 2029 EXIT FEASIBILITY – LEASE STRUCTURE, BREAK CONDITIONS & NEXT STEPS**

**Current Lease Structure & Term**

Your lease commenced on 1 January 2024 for a term of 15 years, expiring on 31 December 2038. The lease contains two contractually defined review dates: 1 January 2029 (the fifth anniversary of commencement) and 1 January 2034 (the tenth anniversary).

**Critically, 2029 is not an automatic lease termination date.** Instead, 1 January 2029 marks a rent review trigger and—more importantly for your exit planning—the first available break date. The lease does not expire naturally at 2029; if you do not exercise a contractual break right at that date, the lease will continue to 31 December 2038 unless terminated by other means (which we address below).

**Break Clauses & Exit Triggers**

You do have a contractual right to exit at 1 January 2029, but it is conditional and must be exercised strictly:

*Mechanics:*
- You may determine the lease on 1 January 2029 (or alternatively on 1 January 2034) by serving written notice on the Landlord in accordance with section 8.2 of the lease.
- You must give **at least 12 months' prior written notice** (a "Break Notice") of your intention to exercise the break. This means the notice must be served by 1 January 2028 at the latest.
- Once a Break Notice is given, it is **irrevocable**—you cannot withdraw it.
- Notice must be served in compliance with Section 196 of the Law of Property Act 1925 (the statutory provisions governing service of notices in property law); we will confirm proper serving procedures with you separately.

*Three Binding Conditions:*

Your right to break on 1 January 2029 is **conditional** on all of the following being satisfied by that date:

1. **No Material Unremedied Breach:** You must not be in material breach of any of your covenants under the lease at the break date. Any material breach that remains unremedied will render your Break Notice ineffective and the lease will continue.

2. **Vacant Possession:** You must give the Landlord vacant possession of the **whole of the Premises**, free from all occupiers, subtenants and other persons. This means the building must be fully unoccupied and available for the Landlord to take back.

3. **Break Premium Payment:** You must pay the Landlord a "Break Premium" equal to **six months' rent at the rate payable immediately before the Break Date**, by cleared funds, on or before 1 January 2029.

If any one of these conditions is not met, your Break Notice will have no effect and the lease will continue to 31 December 2038 with all associated rental and other liabilities.

**The Break Premium and Rent Review Risk**

The Break Premium is a direct cash cost you must budget for. At your current Initial Rent of £850,000 per annum (exclusive of VAT), the Break Premium would be £425,000 (six months). 

**However, this figure will almost certainly be higher.** The lease contains an upward-only rent review at 1 January 2029. The Reviewed Rent is defined as the higher of (a) the rent currently payable (£850,000) and (b) the open market rent of the premises at 1 January 2029, assessed on a willing landlord / willing tenant basis. Given typical office market inflation, the open market rent at 1 January 2029 is likely to exceed £850,000. The Break Premium is then calculated at six months of that *higher* reviewed rate. For example, if the reviewed rent increases to £900,000 per annum, your Break Premium obligation rises to £450,000.

The exact Reviewed Rent cannot be confirmed until 1 January 2029, unless you and the Landlord agree it beforehand or it is determined by an independent surveyor acting as an expert. Until the Reviewed Rent is formally ascertained, you will continue to pay the previous rate (£850,000) plus interest on any shortfall once determined.

**We will need a professional valuation forecast** to estimate the likely open market rent at 1 January 2029, so you can budget for the probable Break Premium cost.

**Exit Costs & Liabilities**

Exit in 2029 will create several categories of cost and liability, beyond the Break Premium:

*Dilapidations and Reinstatement:*

The lease imposes **full repairing obligations** throughout the term, with only fair wear and tear excepted. You must keep the Premises in good and substantial repair and condition, and yield them up in that condition at the end of the lease (or sooner, if determined by break). 

Critically, you must keep the interior of the Premises—including internal surfaces of external and load-bearing walls, floors, ceilings, columns, doors, windows and frames—properly decorated to the standard of "a first-class office building in the City of London." You must redecorate these surfaces **at least once every five years of the term, and also in the last year of the term (howsoever determined)**.

A 2029 exit means **2028 is the last year of the lease term (as determined)**. You must therefore complete a full professional redecoration of all interior surfaces to first-class City standard by 31 December 2028. Failure to do so will constitute a material breach of your repairing covenant and will likely render your Break Notice ineffective.

These redecoration and remedial works are a significant unrecovered cost if the break cannot be exercised. Additionally, if the Premises are in worse condition than set out in the Schedule of Condition (prepared by Carter Mitchell Surveyors LLP at the commencement date on 1 January 2024, and annexed as Schedule 4 to the lease), or if any defects fall outside fair wear and tear, you may face a dilapidations claim from the Landlord after termination.

*Other Direct Costs on Termination:*

- **Final Rent & Service Charge:** You will be liable for rent and service charge up to and including the date of termination (1 January 2029). If the Reviewed Rent is agreed or determined before that date, you will pay the higher rate from 1 January 2029; if not, disputes over rent arrears and interest may arise.
- **Business Rates & Insurance:** You will remain liable for all business rates and insurance premiums until termination, absent any landlord obligations that would otherwise apply.
- **Break Premium:** As noted, six months' rent at the reviewed rate.

*Post-Termination Exposure:*

Even after you leave, the Landlord may make a claim for dilapidations if the condition of the Premises at termination is worse than the Schedule of Condition records, or if remedial works have not been completed to the required standard. These claims can be substantial and may take months or years to resolve.

**Compliance & Operational Barriers**

Your ability to exercise the 2029 break depends critically on your compliance with lease covenants by the break date:

*Repairing and Decoration (Material Risk):*

As detailed above, any material breach of your repairing obligations will prevent break exercise. A dilapidations survey against the Schedule of Condition should be instructed immediately to establish what remedial works and redecoration are required, the cost, and whether these can realistically be completed by 31 December 2028 without significant business disruption or cost overrun.

*Alienation (Assignment & Subletting):*

We have not yet reviewed the full terms of the assignment and subletting provisions in the lease. If you are considering an exit by sale of the lease or assignment to a third party, rather than physical exit, the lease restrictions on alienation (e.g., landlord consent requirements, conditions precedent) must be understood. These may limit your exit options or add cost and delay.

*Use Restrictions:*

We have not yet reviewed any restrictions on use of the Premises or covenants relating to the nature of your business. If the lease contains restrictive use clauses and you have breached them (e.g., by conducting a use not permitted), this may constitute a material breach and prevent break exercise.

*Guarantor Obligations:*

The lease may require a guarantor. If so, guarantor release or consent to lease determination may be required on exit, and this could create a practical or cost barrier.

**Next Steps & Information Needed**

To assess feasibility of a 2029 exit, we need to:

1. **Dilapidations Survey:** Instruct a qualified surveyor to inspect the Premises against the Schedule of Condition (Schedule 4). Identify any defects beyond fair wear and tear and estimate the cost and timeline to remedy each by 1 January 2029. Obtain quotations for a full professional redecoration of all interior surfaces to first-class City office standard, scheduled for 2028.

2. **Valuation Forecast:** Engage a commercial property surveyor to estimate the open market rent of the Premises at 1 January 2029 (on willing landlord / tenant principles, as the lease defines). This will forecast the likely Reviewed Rent and hence the Break Premium.

3. **Landlord Breach Position:** Request the Landlord's current view of whether you are in any breach of your covenants under the lease. Flag to the Landlord your intention to exercise the break at 1 January 2029 and seek early engagement on any alleged breaches, to give time for remediation.

4. **Lease Document Review:** Provide us with the full lease, including all schedules (particularly Schedule 4 – Schedule of Condition) and any amendments or side letters. We will then review the full assignment/subletting restrictions, use covenants, guarantor provisions, and any other material terms affecting exit cost and feasibility.

5. **Business & Occupancy Plan:** Confirm your own timeline for relocation. Can you achieve vacant possession of the entire Premises by 1 January 2029? Are there any practical constraints (e.g., business continuity, alternative premises availability, staff relocation) that would prevent you from vacating by that date?

6. **Breach Compliance Action Plan:** Once the dilapidations survey is complete, develop a detailed action plan and budget to remedy any breaches and complete all redecoration by 31 December 2028. This will inform your realistic ability to meet the break conditions.

7. **Notice Mechanics:** Confirm with us the proper procedure for serving a Break Notice in compliance with Section 196 of the Law of Property Act 1925, and the formal notice deadline (1 January 2028, to provide 12 months' notice of a 1 January 2029 break).

**Outstanding Uncertainties**

The following remain unclear and will be addressed once we receive the full lease and conduct the above enquiries:

- The exact scope of the assignment and subletting restrictions, and whether a lease sale is practically or legally feasible.
- Whether there are any further break dates or termination rights beyond those noted above.
- The full scope of your use covenants and whether any current or planned use falls outside the permitted scope.
- The identity and obligations of any guarantor.
- The precise definition of "material breach" in the lease (the lease does not define this term; disputes may arise on whether a particular breach prevents break exercise).

**Conclusion**

A 2029 exit is contractually possible if you can: (1) satisfy all three break conditions; (2) afford the Break Premium (estimated at £425,000–£450,000 or more, depending on the reviewed rent); and (3) complete all dilapidations and redecoration works by 31 December 2028. If any break condition is not met, the lease will continue to 31 December 2038 with all associated costs and liabilities.

We recommend you prioritize the dilapidations survey, valuation forecast, and landlord engagement on breaches to establish a realistic exit timeline and cost, and confirm your own occupancy and relocation readiness. Once this information is gathered, we will be able to advise on the genuine feasibility of a 2029 exit and any negotiated alternatives with the Landlord (e.g., early lease termination at a reduced premium, landlord consent to assignment, etc.).

---

**This is a draft client update for your review and does not constitute legal advice on your compliance with lease covenants or your ability to exercise the break. The findings and uncertainties set out above will be refined once we receive and review the full lease and the information requested above.**

findings.title: Assignment Consent Mechanism – Landlord Consent Standard and Conditions
findings.interpretation: The tenant may not assign the whole lease without prior written landlord consent, which cannot be unreasonably withheld or delayed. The landlord may impose reasonable conditions, including authorised guarantee agreements. Consent is conditional on the assignee demonstrating sufficient financial standing and respectability to comply with covenants. This framework protects the landlord from occupant transfer to unsuitable parties but contains the 'reasonableness' constraint which may be disputed if the landlord refuses consent without clear grounds.
findings.relevance: Critical to landlord's objective of controlling assignment to protect rental income and occupant suitability. The unreasonableness limitation requires clear articulation of consent criteria during negotiation to avoid future disputes and challenged refusals.
findings.next_step: Negotiate detailed assignment criteria (minimum turnover/credit rating, negative vetting of sector/use compliance, AGA structure and duration) and confirm landlord's right to levy assignment fees or recover transaction costs to establish objective consent grounds.
findings.quote: The Tenant shall not assign the whole or any part of this Lease without the prior written consent of the Landlord, such consent not to be unreasonably withheld or delayed. The Landlord may impose reasonable conditions on any such consent, including (without limitation) a requirement for an authorised guarantee agreement from the outgoing Tenant.
findings.uncertainty: The phrase 'respectable and responsible person or entity' is subjective and may not withstand challenge if the landlord refuses consent on character grounds alone. The scope of 'reasonable conditions' beyond AGA is not exhaustively defined and may require clarification, particularly regarding assignment fees, security top-up, and ongoing guarantor liability.

findings.title: Subletting Whole – Upward-Only Rent Review and Lease Consistency Requirement
findings.interpretation: The tenant may sublet the whole premises only with landlord consent (not to be unreasonably withheld) and the sub-lease must contain upward-only rent review at intervals of no more than 5 years and must otherwise be consistent with the head lease terms. Part subletting is prohibited entirely. This protects the landlord from income loss through downward rent-fixing on a subtenancy and prevents piecemeal occupation loss, but the requirement that subleases be 'consistent' with the head lease may trigger disputes about which terms apply and whether secondary occupant restrictions are enforceable.
findings.relevance: Directly supports landlord's objective to control occupancy and prevent loss of rental income if tenant relocates. The upward-only rent floor protects landlord's income base during subleases, but partial subletting prohibition needs enforcement and monitoring.
findings.next_step: Obtain sample sub-lease pro-forma to confirm consistency requirement is workable (e.g., whether alienation, insurance, repair, and service charge pass-through are enforceable against subtenants). Confirm landlord consent process for subleases and whether variation/amendment consent is required during subtenancy term.
findings.quote: Any subletting shall be by way of a sub-lease which contains provisions for upward only rent review at intervals of not more than five (5) years, and which otherwise contains provisions consistent with the terms of this Lease.
findings.uncertainty: The definition of 'provisions consistent with the terms of this Lease' is not exhaustively stated. It is unclear whether covenants regarding use, alterations, insurance, repair and service charge reimbursement are automatically incorporated into subleases or require express adoption. Landlord's enforcement rights against subtenants (e.g., for breach of use or repair) are not addressed in this clause.

findings.title: Rent Review Mechanism at Years 5 and 10 – Upward-Only Expert Determination
findings.interpretation: Rent reviews occur on 1 January 2029 and 1 January 2034. The mechanism is upward-only (no reduction). Initial rent is £850,000 p.a. exclusive of VAT. If parties do not agree the Reviewed Rent by the Review Date, an independent surveyor (appointed by agreement or by RICS President on application) acts as expert (not arbitrator) to determine the reviewed rent. During the review period, the tenant continues to pay the pre-review rate, with backpayment of shortfall plus interest at 2% above Barclays base rate within 14 days of ascertainment. The mechanism provides upside protection for the landlord but lacks a defined methodology (e.g., CPI indexation, market comparables, formula).
findings.relevance: Central to landlord's rental income protection strategy. Upward-only mechanism and expert determination protect against market downturns and ensure income growth, but absence of a formula or reference rate creates uncertainty and potential for expert determiner disagreement, triggering cost and delay.
findings.next_step: Agree with tenant on review methodology before lease completion: fixed percentage increase, RPI/CPI indexation cap-and-collar, or open market valuation by reference to specified comparables and assumptions. Establish cost allocation (proportionate bearing or tenant bears all expert fees if rent increase exceeds stated threshold) to reduce risk of protracted disputes.
findings.quote: In default of agreement between the Landlord and the Tenant as to the Reviewed Rent by the relevant Review Date, the Reviewed Rent shall be determined by an independent surveyor acting as an expert (and not as an arbitrator) appointed by agreement between the parties or, in default of agreement, by the President for the time being of the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors on the application of either party. The rent review shall be upward only.
findings.uncertainty: The lease does not specify the basis for the expert's valuation (comparable market rents, investment yield, inflation-linked floor, or tenant's ability to pay). The term 'upward only' does not specify a floor (e.g., minimum of initial rent or RPI-linked baseline). The timing of expert determination (particularly if appointed late) and the consequent cash-flow recovery period for backpayment is not quantified. Tenant continues to pay the old rent during review, which may create shortfall arrears if the expert's decision is delayed beyond the Review Date.

findings.title: Tenant Break Rights – Conditional on No Material Breach, Vacant Possession, and Break Premium
findings.interpretation: The tenant may break the lease on 1 January 2029 (5 years) or 1 January 2034 (10 years) by serving 12 months' prior irrevocable notice under Section 196 LPA 1925. The right is conditional on: (1) no material unremedied breach by tenant at Break Date; (2) vacant possession of the entire premises free from occupiers and subtenants; and (3) payment of a Break Premium equal to 6 months' rent at the pre-break rate. If conditions are not satisfied, the Break Notice is void and the lease continues. This framework gives the tenant significant exit rights that expose the landlord to occupancy uncertainty and early lease termination, but the conditions create enforcement leverage.
findings.relevance: Material to landlord's long-term rental income security and lease duration planning. The tenant's break rights create two junctures (years 5 and 10) where the full rent and service charge could be lost, necessitating contingency planning for alternative lettings or lease renewal. The Break Premium of 6 months' rent provides partial compensation but is unlikely to offset transaction costs or extended void periods.
findings.next_step: Assess whether Break Premium is adequate for re-letting costs, agent commissions, and landlord legal fees (typically 15–20% of annual rent plus void holding costs). Consider negotiating increase to Break Premium (e.g., 9–12 months' rent) or introducing a rent abatement suspension (i.e., no rent reduction if break notice is served). Confirm enforcement mechanism for 'material breach' and 'vacant possession' conditions to ensure tenant compliance.
findings.quote: The Tenant may determine this Lease on the fifth (5th) anniversary of the Term Commencement Date (being 1 January 2029) or the tenth (10th) anniversary of the Term Commencement Date (being 1 January 2034) (each a "Break Date") by serving written notice on the Landlord in accordance with clause 8.2. [The Tenant's] right to determine this Lease on a Break Date shall be conditional upon the following conditions being satisfied on or before the relevant Break Date: (a) there is no material breach by the Tenant of any of the Tenant's covenants in this Lease which remains unremedied at the Break Date; (b) the Tenant gives vacant possession of the whole of the Premises to the Landlord on or before the Break Date, free from all occupiers, subtenants and other persons claiming through or under the Tenant; (c) the Tenant pays to the Landlord on or before the Break Date a sum equivalent to six (6) months' rent at the rate payable immediately before the Break Date.
findings.uncertainty: The meaning of 'material breach' is not defined and may be disputed (e.g., whether minor late payment, minor decoration default, or service charge arrears qualify). The timing and process for rectification of material breach are not specified—whether the tenant can cure within a grace period post-Break Date or whether breach must be remedied before Break Notice is served is unclear. The 'vacant possession' requirement is strict (no subtenants) which will require active monitoring and enforcement, particularly if the tenant has permitted short-term occupiers.

findings.title: Repair and Maintenance Allocation – Tenant Interior and Landlord Structure with Service Charge Recovery
findings.interpretation: Tenant is responsible for keeping the interior of the premises (including internal surfaces of external and load-bearing walls, floors, ceilings, columns, doors, windows and frames) in good repair, fair wear and tear excepted, and for redecoration at least once every 5 years and in the final year of the term. The landlord is responsible for structure and exterior (including roof, foundations, external walls, common parts) and all plant and machinery (lifts, air conditioning, fire systems, common lighting). Tenant's repairing obligations are limited by a schedule of condition (Schedule 4, prepared by Carter Mitchell Surveyors LLP at Term Commencement). Landlord's structural and building costs are recovered as a service charge, with tenant's proportion at 18.7% of total building lettable area. This allocation is typical but places significant cost exposure on the landlord for major structural remedies and building plant, with recovery dependent on service charge collection and tenant solvency.
findings.relevance: Key to landlord's objective of minimizing cost exposure and ensuring tenant contribution to building maintenance. The service charge mechanism is the primary tool for cost recovery, but the 18.7% proportion depends on building occupancy and other tenants' solvency. Schedule of condition protects against tenant claims for pre-existing damage but may limit tenant's repairing obligation if the premises are in poor condition at commencement.
findings.next_step: Confirm that Schedule 4 (schedule of condition) is comprehensive and accurately reflects the state of Floors 8–10 at 1 January 2024, with photographs and detailed defect register to avoid later disputes about baseline condition. Agree service charge cap or indexation clause to control tenant's exposure and incentivize landlord cost management. Verify that redecoration cycle (once per 5 years, plus final year) is enforceable and that tenant's decoration standard ('first-class office building in the City of London') is objectively measurable.
findings.quote: The Tenant shall keep the interior of the Premises (including the internal surfaces of all external and load-bearing walls, floors, ceilings, columns, doors, windows and window frames) properly decorated to a standard consistent with that of a first-class office building in the City of London, and shall redecorate the same not less frequently than once in every five (5) years of the Term and in the last year of the Term (howsoever determined). [The Landlord shall] maintain, repair and as necessary renew all plant, machinery and equipment serving the Building, including the lifts, air conditioning system, fire detection and suppression systems, and common area lighting. The cost of the Landlord's obligations under this clause 4.2 shall be recoverable from the Tenant as part of the service charge in accordance with Schedule 3 hereto, the Tenant's proportion being 18.7%.
findings.uncertainty: The definition of 'fair wear and tear excepted' is not detailed—what constitutes normal wear versus tenant-caused damage may be disputed at lease end. The standard of 'first-class office building' is subjective and may not be enforceable without reference to a comparables standard or surveyor's assessment. The service charge mechanism (Schedule 3) is not reproduced in full, so the dispute-resolution process for contested service charge bills, treatment of estimated vs. actual costs, and landlord's recovery rights for shortfalls are unknown. The tenant's proportion (18.7%) assumes current building occupancy and lettable area—if other tenants vacate or areas are converted, this proportion may be recalculated, creating tenant resentment and potential disputes.

findings.title: Permitted Use Restriction to Class E(g)(i) Offices – No Licensing or Disturbance Clause Enforcement
findings.interpretation: The tenant must use the premises solely for Class E(g)(i) use (offices) and for no other purpose. The use definition is pinned to the Town and Country Planning (Use Classes) Order 1987 (as amended). The lease also restricts use to purposes that do not, in the landlord's reasonable opinion, constitute a nuisance, annoyance or disturbance. These restrictions protect the landlord from incompatible occupancy (e.g., nightclub, industrial, heavy manufacturing) but the 'reasonable opinion' standard may be disputed and enforcement requires monitoring and forfeiture action. There is no express condition requiring tenant to obtain and maintain planning permission or licensing (e.g., for Licensing Act 2003 regulated activity) and no obligation for tenant to notify landlord of material change in use or regulatory compliance.
findings.relevance: Supports the landlord's objective of controlling occupancy suitability and protecting the building's market positioning and other tenants' enjoyment. Meridian Consulting Group LLP is proposed to use the premises for consulting services (consistent with Class E(g)(i)), but the lease lacks an express verification of current use and no mechanism to monitor ongoing use compliance.
findings.next_step: Obtain from tenant confirmation of its specific operations (consulting disciplines, client types, employee numbers, any ancillary activities such as events, training, manufacturing sample production) to assess use class compliance and any potential disturbance (noise, traffic, hours of operation, visitor footfall). Establish a use compliance certification requirement (annual or bi-annual tenant confirmation) and reserve landlord's right to audit use. Clarify whether Meridian's permitted use includes home-working for employees or guest office arrangements, which may affect occupancy loading and service load.
findings.quote: The Tenant shall use the Premises for the Permitted Use only and for no other purpose whatsoever. The Permitted Use shall be limited to use falling within Class E(g)(i) of the Town and Country Planning (Use Classes) Order 1987 (as amended), being use as offices.
findings.uncertainty: The lease does not define what activities fall within Class E(g)(i) or confirm that Meridian's current business model (consulting) is confined to that class. There is no express requirement for the tenant to maintain planning permission or change of use consent, or to notify the landlord of any application or enforcement action by local planning authority. The clause 6.1 reference to 'reasonable opinion' on nuisance/annoyance is subjective and has not been tested by reference to specific industries, noise levels, hours, or traffic generation. There is no express procedure for landlord inspection or tenant audit to verify ongoing use compliance.

gaps: Deposit and parent company guarantee: No information provided on the amount of deposit, form (cash or undertaking), refundability terms, parent company guarantee structure (if any), or scope of guarantor liability (full lease term or limited period). This is critical for landlord's security against tenant default and dilapidations claims at lease end.

Service charge detail and dispute resolution: Schedule 3 (referenced in clause 4.2.3 for service charge mechanism) has not been read. The lease lacks detail on service charge cap, indexation, tenant's right to challenge service charge bills, dispute resolution process, and landlord's recovery rights for arrears and interest.

Insurance covenants and excess allocation: Clause 5 outlines landlord's insurance obligation and tenant's reimbursement proportion (18.7%), but does not specify whether tenant is liable for policy excess (particularly high-value claims) or whether increased premiums from tenant activities are passed through. Tenant's environmental indemnity (clause 9.2) is broad but enforcement against tenant solvency is not addressed.

Forfeiture and default remedies: The lease does not explicitly address landlord's forfeiture rights for material breach, notice period for remedying breach, landlord's rights to take emergency action (e.g., repair and charge back to tenant), or interest rates on arrears beyond the rent review shortfall (2% above Barclays base rate). Standard forfeiture protections under the Law of Property Act 1925 Section 146 are assumed but not stated.

Tenant's financial standing and operational details: No financial information provided on Meridian Consulting Group LLP (turnover, EBITDA, credit rating, parent company support, industry sector, employee numbers, or lease expense ratio). This is essential for assessing credit risk and negotiating appropriate AGA scope, deposit level, and break premium amount.

Assignment and subletting fees: The lease does not specify whether the landlord may charge a professional fee for considering assignment or subletting consent requests, or whether the tenant bears the landlord's legal and surveyor costs. Industry practice often permits landlord cost recovery (typically £500–2,000 plus disbursements).

Schedule 4 (Schedule of Condition): The lease references a schedule of condition prepared by Carter Mitchell Surveyors LLP but the document has not been read or reviewed. This schedule is critical as it defines the baseline condition of the premises and limits tenant's repairing obligations. Its adequacy and accuracy should be verified before lease completion.

Rent review provisions – methodology and comparables: The lease does not specify the methodology for the expert surveyor's determination of Reviewed Rent (e.g., comparable market evidence, investment yield, inflation baseline, tenant's ability to pay). This is a major gap that should be resolved through negotiation to avoid uncertainty at the 2029 and 2034 review dates.

cases.draft:
ASSIGNMENT & SUBLETTING CONTROL

**1. ASSIGNMENT CONSENT MECHANISM**

The lease requires the tenant (Meridian Consulting Group LLP) to obtain the landlord's prior written consent before assigning the whole lease. Under the current draft, landlord consent cannot be unreasonably withheld or delayed, and the landlord may impose reasonable conditions—including an authorised guarantee agreement (AGA)—as a condition of consent.

The lease requires that any assignee demonstrate "sufficient financial standing and respectability" to comply with the lease covenants. This framework is intended to protect the landlord from assignment to unsuitable occupants, but contains two material uncertainties:

- **Subjectivity of "respectability"**: The phrase does not define objective criteria. Refusal of consent based on character grounds alone may be challenged as unreasonable if the landlord cannot articulate documented concerns about the assignee's ability or willingness to perform covenants. The reasonableness constraint may require the landlord to justify refusal by reference to financial position, sector, or regulatory status, rather than subjective reputation assessment.

- **Scope of "reasonable conditions"**: The lease permits "reasonable conditions" but does not exhaustively define what conditions are permissible beyond AGA. This creates scope for dispute if the landlord seeks to impose assignment fees, security top-up, extended guarantor liability, or other transaction-related costs.

**Negotiation Position**: 

To strengthen the landlord's control and reduce future disputes:

(1) Establish objective assignment consent criteria in the lease (or side letter) including:
   - Minimum turnover and credit rating thresholds proportionate to annual rent (£850,000 p.a. exclusive of VAT at commencement).
   - Negative vetting (e.g., not in prohibited sectors, no regulatory restrictions, no related-party transactions reducing independence).
   - Verification of assignee's track record of lease compliance and rent payment (reference checks).

(2) Clarify the scope of conditions:
   - Confirm landlord's right to require AGA from the outgoing tenant for the full remainder of the term (not time-limited).
   - Define whether assignment fees or transaction cost recovery (legal/valuation) are permissible and, if so, at what level.
   - State whether landlord may require security deposit adjustment if the assignee's credit profile differs materially from the original tenant.

(3) Specify the consent process and timeline (e.g., landlord to respond to properly documented application within 10 working days; silence deemed consent if landlord fails to respond with reasons within agreed period).

**Information Gap**: Obtain from Meridian Consulting Group LLP: (i) confirmation of current turnover and credit rating; (ii) identification of any related-party entities that may assign without arm's-length vetting; (iii) sector/regulatory status to confirm fit with landlord's permitted use requirement (Class E(g)(i) offices) and any covenant restrictions.

---

**2. SUBLETTING WHOLE PREMISES – UPWARD-ONLY RENT AND CONSISTENCY REQUIREMENT**

The lease permits subletting of the **whole premises only** with landlord consent (not to be unreasonably withheld). Any sub-lease must contain:

- **Upward-only rent review** at intervals of no more than 5 years.
- **Provisions consistent with the terms of the head lease**.

**Part subletting is prohibited entirely**, which protects the landlord from piecemeal occupation loss and fractured covenant enforcement.

Upward-only rent on subleases protects the landlord's income floor: if the tenant sublets, the rent payable to the landlord cannot be reduced in the subtenancy market downturn. However, the requirement that subleases contain provisions "consistent with the terms of this Lease" introduces two material uncertainties:

- **Scope of "consistency"**: The lease does not exhaustively define which head lease terms must be incorporated into subleases. It is unclear whether covenants regarding use (Class E(g)(i) offices only), alterations, insurance, repair, and service charge reimbursement are automatically binding on subtenants or require express adoption in the sub-lease. If consistency is interpreted narrowly, the landlord may be unable to enforce use restrictions or repair obligations against subtenants, creating secondary occupancy risk.

- **Enforcement against subtenants**: The head lease does not address the landlord's direct enforcement rights against subtenants for breach of use, repair, or other covenants. If the tenant fails to enforce the sub-lease against a subtenant, the landlord's recourse is limited to action against the tenant for head lease breach, leaving a gap in occupancy control.

**Negotiation Position**:

(1) Define "consistency" by reference to a sub-lease pro-forma (to be attached to the lease or prepared before completion):
   - Confirm that use restriction (Class E(g)(i) offices only, no other use without landlord consent) applies to subtenants.
   - Require subtenants to covenant to maintain and repair their occupied demise to the same standard as the head lease.
   - State that service charge and insurance reimbursement obligations pass through to subtenants on the same basis as the head lease.
   - Include an assignment/subletting restriction on the sub-lease preventing further subletting without landlord consent.

(2) Reserve landlord's direct enforcement rights:
   - Confirm that the landlord may serve notice directly on the subtenant of any use breach or repair default and require rectification within a specified period.
   - Alternatively, reserve the right to forfeit the head lease for the tenant's failure to enforce the sub-lease against a subtenant's material breach.

(3) Confirm the consent process for subletting (timing, information required from tenant about proposed subtenant, and any inspection rights).

**Information Gap**: (i) Identify whether Meridian Consulting Group LLP anticipates subletting any part of Floors 8–10 during the 15-year term, and if so, for what purpose and anticipated duration. (ii) Confirm the proposed sub-lease term length (is it fixed, or terminable at will, exposing the landlord to intermittent re-letting risk?). (iii) Obtain any draft sub-lease pro-forma to verify alignment with head lease repair, use, and service charge obligations.

---

**3. ASSIGNMENT AND SUBLETTING – STRUCTURAL GAPS AND MISSING INFORMATION**

The lease does not address:

- **Profit-sharing on assignment**: There is no express provision permitting the landlord to share in any profit or premium realized by the tenant on assignment. Market-standard clauses often require the assignee to pay an "assignment premium" or require profit-sharing (e.g., 50% of any value uplift above the initial rent) to compensate the landlord for covenant loss risk. Insertion of such a clause would strengthen the landlord's incentive to control the assignee pool and capture upside from occupancy value.

- **Forfeiture for breach of alienation restrictions**: The lease does not explicitly address whether the tenant's breach of assignment or subletting restrictions (e.g., assignment without consent or subletting part premises) triggers forfeiture rights. Confirmation that such breaches constitute material breach, entitling the landlord to forfeit, is critical to enforcement.

- **Guarantor liability post-assignment**: It is not stated whether the outgoing tenant remains liable as guarantor after assignment, or whether the AGA limits that liability to the immediate successor tenant only. Clarification is needed to establish the depth of the covenant chain.

**Negotiation Position**: Propose amendments to (i) introduce assignment profit-sharing or assignment fee; (ii) confirm that breach of alienation restrictions triggers forfeiture rights; (iii) clarify the duration and scope of AGA liability (recommend AGA covers the immediate successor only, to preserve incentive for careful vetting of assignee).

---

**SUMMARY OF NEGOTIATING PRIORITIES – ASSIGNMENT & SUBLETTING**

| Issue | Current Position | Risk | Negotiation Objective |
|-------|------------------|------|----------------------|
| **Assignment Consent Criteria** | Subjective "respectability" test; "reasonable conditions" undefined | Dispute over consent refusal; uncontrolled assignment fees | Establish objective consent criteria (turnover, credit, sector, use compliance) and expressly permit security top-up and extended AGA |
| **Subletting Consistency** | Subleases must be "consistent" with head lease; part subletting prohibited | Enforcement gap against subtenants; use and repair covenants may not bind subtenants | Attach sub-lease pro-forma defining use, repair, and service charge pass-through; reserve landlord's direct enforcement rights against subtenants |
| **Assignment Profit-Sharing** | Not addressed in current draft | Loss of upside if tenant realizes value uplift on assignment | Propose 50% profit-sharing or assignment premium to capture occupancy value and align tenant incentives |
| **Forfeiture for Alienation Breach** | Not explicit in current draft | Uncertainty whether unauthorized assignment or part-subletting justifies forfeiture | Confirm expressly that breach of alienation restrictions is material breach triggering forfeiture rights |
| **Guarantor Liability Chain** | Not specified whether AGA limits liability to immediate successor | Exposure to assignee default if liability chain breaks | Clarify that AGA covers immediate successor; consider security top-up on assignment to offset new occupant risk |

---

**OUTSTANDING INFORMATION REQUIRED**

Before finalizing assignment and subletting terms, obtain clarification from Meridian Consulting Group LLP and legal advisers:

1. **Meridian's Anticipated Occupancy Model**: Does Meridian expect to occupy the entire demise (Floors 8–10) as single-entity offices throughout the 15-year term, or are there plans to relocate, sublet, or assign before the term end?

2. **Related-Party or Subsidiary Assignment Risk**: Are there any immediate plans for Meridian to transfer the lease to a related-party entity, parent company, or subsidiary?
